extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys and other practitioners who appear before the USPTO; Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) staff; attorneys facing reciprocal discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules the USPTO applies when deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a final adjudication in another jurisdiction, including the respondent's burden to show a genuine issue of material fact under Selling v. Radford and 37 C.F.R. § 11.24. Also covers related practitioner obligations (limited recognition, wind-up duties, notice, and reinstatement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling v. Radford presumption for reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: State disbarment creates a federal presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper unless an independent review reveals: (1) a want of due process due to lack of notice or opportunity to be heard; (2) an infirmity of proof of misconduct; or (3) that grave injustice would result from the imposition of reciprocal discipline. (Selling v. Radford, 243 U.S. 46 (1917)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal precedent places the burden on the respondent to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline. Courts have generally required the respondent to make that showing by clear and convincing evidence (citing In re Kramer, 282 F.3d 721). The USPTO follows this framework in evaluating reciprocal-discipline petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d) — Director's default rule and carve-outs
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical suspension unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the Director finds, there is a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process; (ii) there was such infirmity of proof as to give rise to the conviction that the Office could not accept the conclusion; (iii) imposition of the same suspension would result in grave injustice; or (iv) any argument that the practitioner was not suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must file a timely response identifying factual/material disputes tied to these four specific grounds. The Director will accept the foreign adjudication as conclusive unless one of these narrow exceptions is established clearly and convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(e) — prima facie case from a final adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: A final adjudication in another jurisdiction that a practitioner has been guilty of misconduct establishes a prima facie case by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner violated 37 C.F.R. 10.23 (as further identified under 10.23(c)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A foreign disciplinary order creates a strong presumption that applicable USPTO ethical rules were violated; the Office treats the state finding as establishing a prima facie violation subject to the respondent's narrow rebuttal under § 11.24(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23 (ethical standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that 'reflects adversely upon a practitioner's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a lawyer' (10.23(b)), and conduct involving 'dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation' (10.23(d)), are bases for discipline; 10.23(c)(5) is referenced for further identification of applicable misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a foreign adjudication finds violations that map to § 10.23 grounds (e.g., furnishing liquor to minors, sexual misconduct with a minor by a custodian, or dishonesty), those findings typically satisfy the prima facie case under § 11.24(e). The Office will examine whether the foreign adjudication actually establishes the mapped § 10.23 violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's duty to file a timely, fact-specific response
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notice and Order pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 requires the respondent to file, within the time specified (40 days in this matter), a response containing all information the respondent believes sufficient to establish a genuine issue of material fact under § 11.24(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses must identify and support (with documents, affidavits, deposition excerpts, etc.) any claimed infirmity of proof, due process defect, or grave injustice. Vague disagreement or unsupported assertions will not meet the clear-and-convincing showing required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent bears the burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements (lack of due process, infirmity of proof, or grave injustice) applies to preclude imposition of reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office applies a high evidentiary standard. Mere allegations, timeline disputes, or contrary findings by investigative agencies do not, without clear and convincing support, create a genuine issue of material fact sufficient to avoid reciprocal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural due process defined as notice and opportunity to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural due process in this context means the state disciplinary proceeding provided notice and an opportunity to be heard (participation in discovery, hearing, and post-hearing correction procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish a due-process deprivation the respondent must show the proceeding was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation; participation in discovery, hearings, and opportunities to request correction weigh against a due-process claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof — what will and will not suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: An infirmity of proof claim must show such weakness in the evidence supporting the foreign adjudication that the USPTO could not accept the conclusion as final. Mere disagreement, differing investigative outcomes in other agencies, or later testimony do not automatically establish infirmity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office gives weight to stipulated facts and hearing officer findings relied upon by the foreign tribunal. Evidence that other agencies declined action does not necessarily undercut the state court's later findings, especially when stipulations post-date those investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice — narrow, demanding standard; financial hardship insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid reciprocal discipline on the basis of grave injustice, the respondent must clearly and convincingly show that imposition of the same suspension by the USPTO would result in grave injustice to the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office explicitly states that loss of income and ordinary financial hardship resulting from suspension are not sufficient to establish grave injustice, because financial consequences naturally flow from suspension. Alleged harms to clients do not substitute for a showing of grave injustice to the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office's evaluative responsibility for practitioners' character
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has a statutory responsibility to assure that those who represent parties before the Office are of sound moral character and reputation (35 U.S.C. § 32 and implementing regs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This public-protection duty supports imposition of reciprocal discipline when a foreign adjudication demonstrates conduct that reflects adversely on honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness, even if the misconduct occurred outside the practice of patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition and wind-up duties during the grace period
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may grant limited recognition for a short period (here, 30 days) to wind up client business; during such limited recognition the respondent must wind up client matters, withdraw from employment in pending proceedings per 37 C.F.R. § 10.40, and not accept new clients before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the limited-recognition window the practitioner is directed to withdraw from pending matters and avoid accepting new clients with matters before USPTO. Failure to comply with the wind-up obligations can be actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice obligations to the OED Director
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must notify the OED Director within 30 days of being suspended by another jurisdiction or being disciplinarily disqualified from participating in or appearing before any Federal program or agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely notify the OED Director of comparable suspensions or disqualifications may weigh against the respondent and undermine arguments that reciprocal discipline is unwarranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement eligibility and compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.60
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 after expiration of the suspension (the Office noted eligibility to apply two years from the effective date in this case), and must comply with the procedures of § 11.60 when seeking reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinstatement follows the regulatory process in § 11.60; the practitioner must meet any conditions and procedural requirements set forth there before practice before the Office may be resumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of stipulations of fact and state tribunal findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Stipulations of fact submitted in state disciplinary proceedings and the state tribunal's reliance on hearing officer findings are afforded significant weight; such stipulations can form the evidentiary basis for the state court's findings and for the USPTO's prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent stipulated to facts that formed the basis of the state court's conclusions, the fact of stipulation limits the respondent's ability to later assert infirmity of proof. The Office will examine whether the stipulations actually support the foreign adjudication's conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of foreign criminal-statute definitions when assessing misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When a foreign adjudication relies on criminal statutes (e.g., West Virginia Code definitions such as the statutory definition of 'custodian'), the Office will consider those statutory definitions and the foreign tribunal's application as part of the proof establishing misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A respondent claiming the foreign court misapplied a criminal statute must present clear and convincing evidence of that misapplication to create a genuine issue of material fact. Mere assertion of statutory ambiguity without supporting legal analysis or evidence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural publication and notice to interested parties upon suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: When reciprocal discipline is imposed, the OED Director shall publish notice in the Official Gazette and give notice of the Final Order to appropriate USPTO employees, interested departments, agencies, courts of the United States, and appropriate state authorities where the respondent is known to be a member of the bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and notification are standard administrative steps following a final order; they serve to inform stakeholders and enforce the Office's duty to protect the public and the integrity of representation before USPTO.
